title: High-Throughput Streaming Log Processor
context:
Trading infrastructure talks in logs: every order gateway, matching engine and market-data feed writes millions of CSV lines a day, and the on-call engineer needs answers from them in seconds — not from a Hadoop job. The classic first assignment on an exchange-technology team is exactly this: a single-pass streaming processor that eats a huge log on stdin and emits per-service latency statistics plus anomaly flags, fast enough to run in a pipeline.

The constraints that make it interesting are real: you may not buffer the input, you must survive malformed lines without dying, and throughput is a graded feature — the difference between 200k and 2M lines/sec is the difference between a tool people use and a tool people route around.
problem:
Build a C++17 command-line tool `logproc` that reads a CSV log stream on stdin with lines of the form `timestamp_ms,service,value` (value = response time in ms), maintains rolling per-service statistics with Welford's algorithm, flags anomalies, and writes a summary to stdout.

- **Aggregates per service**: count, mean, population stddev, min, max — printed after EOF as CSV.
- **Flags anomalies**: any observation whose z-score against the *running* mean/stddev exceeds 3 in absolute value after a warm-up of at least 30 observations for that service; anomaly lines are written to stderr in stream order with timestamp, service, value and z-score.
- **Robustness**: blank lines skipped, malformed lines counted and reported in the summary, no crashes on huge or truncated final lines.
- **Performance**: sustained throughput of at least 1M lines/sec on a reference laptop for plain CSV; you must measure and report throughput (lines/sec and MB/s) and explain where the time goes.
requirements: Single-pass streaming: memory per service is O(1) (a Welford accumulator plus counters); the tool never buffers the stream or the output.
Parsing: manual field splitting with `std::from_chars` for integers/doubles (or `strtod`); no iostream extraction (`>>`) in the hot path; a malformed-line counter is included in the summary output.
Correct statistics: Welford mean and *population* stddev per service plus min/max; a documented cross-check against a Python reference implementation on at least 10k lines agrees to 1e-9 relative.

Anomaly detection: |z| > 3 using running statistics with warm-up of at least 30 observations per service; anomalies streamed to stderr in order; the warm-up rule and running-stats semantics are documented (they differ from a two-pass z-score).
Throughput: measured with a generator script over at least 10M lines; report lines/sec and MB/s; stdin is read in large blocks (>= 64 KB) rather than line-by-line `std::getline` on `std::cin`.
Robust I/O: handles EOF without a trailing newline, extremely long lines, and empty input (empty input produces a valid empty summary and exit code 0).
Unit tests for the accumulator and parser (assert-based or CTest) plus one end-to-end test on a fixture file with known expected summary values.

designGuidance.text: Read the stream in blocks, not lines

designGuidance.md: Per-line `std::getline` on `std::cin` synchronises with C stdio and copies repeatedly. The standard fast pattern: `fread` into a 64–256 KB buffer, scan for newlines, and handle the tail that straddles buffer boundaries by carrying the partial line to the front. This one change typically moves a CSV reader from ~300k to several million lines/sec.

designGuidance.caption: Carry the partial line across buffer boundaries

designGuidance.title: Running z-scores are not two-pass z-scores
designGuidance.md: With running statistics, an early outlier inflates the variance and *hides* later anomalies; with two-pass statistics you cannot stream. This project deliberately picks the streaming semantics — document that choice and the warm-up window, because the anomaly list changes with it. There is no 'correct' answer; there is a defensible, stated one.

rows: poor for large mean, small variance

items: **Parsing** dominates once I/O is buffered: `from_chars` for doubles is 3-10x faster than `strtod` and far faster than `std::istringstream`.
**Avoid allocations per line**: split fields with index arithmetic into string_view spans; never construct `std::string` per field in the hot loop.
**Branch predictability**: order checks cheapest-first (field count, then numeric parse); malformed lines should not slow the happy path.
**Measure before optimising**: generate a fixed 10M-line file, time end-to-end, then change one thing at a time.

designGuidance.caption: Pipeline usage: summary on stdout, anomaly stream on stderr

starterFiles.content:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(logproc CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

add_executable(logproc src/main.cpp)
target_include_directories(logproc PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
target_compile_options(logproc PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra -O2)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Statistical correctness (Welford aggregation, min/max, summary fields) verified by cross-check
Anomaly detection semantics: documented choice, warm-up behaviour, planted-anomaly tests
Throughput: measurement methodology, achieved lines/sec, and honest accounting of the hot path
Robustness: malformed input, EOF, empty stream, long lines; no crashes or leaks
Documentation: usage, format contract, benchmark table with hardware

documentationRequirements: README.md: build, usage examples (stdin pipeline and file redirect), exact input/output format contracts including the anomaly stream.
A short DESIGN.md explaining the streaming-semantics choice for anomalies and the warm-up rule.
Benchmark section: generator description, machine, compiler flags, lines/sec and MB/s, plus a note on what limited throughput.
extensionChallenges: Add a second aggregation dimension (per-service-per-minute buckets) without breaking O(1) memory per key — this needs an eviction policy; document it.
Replace the parser with a SIMD-assisted number scanner (or benchmark `from_chars` vs `strtod` at `-O3`) and quantify the gain.
Parallelise with N reader threads feeding shard-partitioned accumulators; prove the result equals the serial run on a fixed input.
